 For a desk that shares one keyboard and mouse between two computers, a 4-port USB 3.0 switch with a wired desk controller is the sensible default from this UGREEN set, and the 10 Gbps USB-C listings are the upgrade when an external SSD rides along. The ten listings below range from a plain USB 2.0 box to 7-port models with USB-C ports and a power adapter. Because every title comes from the same brand, the real differences are the link speed, the port types, the cables in the box and whether power is supplied separately. Those are the points to compare, and they are the points this guide sticks to.

 How these switches differ from a plain hub
 See also: Best UGREEN Webcams for PC: Five Listings Sorted by Resolution, Autofocus and Desk Fit • Best UGREEN KVM Switches for Shared Monitors, Keyboards and Mice 
 A hub splits one port into several for one computer. A switch connects a set of devices to one of two computers at a time, and a button or remote decides which. The idea suits anyone who keeps a work laptop and a personal desktop on the same desk and would rather not reach behind either one to move a cable. From an ergonomics angle, the gain is one keyboard and one mouse at one comfortable position instead of two sets competing for space.
 Titles in this set show three generations of the idea. Older entries stay on USB 2.0 or 5 Gbps USB 3.0 with USB-A cables. Newer ones put USB-C on the computer side, quote 10 Gbps, and add extras such as a built-in network adapter or a file-sync feature. Which generation you need depends mainly on whether a storage drive will share the switch.
 How the list was put together
 Each listing was read for what its title states: link speed, port count, port types, included cables and whether a controller, remote or power adapter ships in the box. Sources are published specifications, manufacturer documentation and buyer reviews. Nobody on the team used or measured these units. Anything the title does not say is marked as a listing question rather than guessed.
 The ten listings
 UGREEN 4-Port USB 3.0 Switch with Controller (USB C and A)
 This is the most flexible entry for a mixed desk. The title mentions both USB C and A devices, four downstream ports, two USB 3.0 cables and a controller, which is the small wired pad that sits on the desk and flips the connection. A USB 3.0 link is nominally 5 Gbps, enough for a keyboard, mouse, webcam and a portable drive used one at a time. If one computer is a USB-C-only laptop, confirm the adapter or cable type in the box.
 It overlaps heavily with the one-button USB 3.0 listing further down, so the controller is the main difference you can verify from the titles.
 A practical scenario: a home-office desk with a work laptop on the left and a personal tower on the right, one keyboard, one mouse, and a webcam that both machines need for calls. The controller lives beside the keyboard, one press moves everything, and the webcam is ready on the other side without unplugging anything. Question to ask before buying: which of the two cables in the box matches the laptop port?
 Pros 
 Controller can sit next to the keyboard
 5 Gbps link class suits drives
 Both USB-C and USB-A devices mentioned
 Cons 
 Power source is not stated in the title
 Bus-powered drives plus a webcam may strain it
 UGREEN USB 2.0 Switch Selector, 4 Devices, One-Button
 The only USB 2.0 model here, aimed at keyboards, mice, scanners and printers. USB 2.0 is 480 Mbps nominal, plenty for input devices and a printer, and noticeably limiting for a modern external drive. The cables are USB A to A, so both computers need a full-size USB-A port. A newer laptop with only USB-C ports will need an adapter that the title does not mention.
 Choose it when speed is irrelevant and cost is the priority. Skip it the moment a portable SSD enters the picture.
 A realistic use is a shared office corner where one printer, one scanner and a basic keyboard serve a desktop and a spare laptop. Nothing in that list needs more than USB 2.0. Question to ask before buying: does either computer lack a full-size USB-A port? If so, an adapter changes the cost picture and the cleaner answer may be one of the C-capable boxes.
 Pros 
 Simple one-button swapping
 Fine for printers and scanners
 Two cables included
 Cons 
 480 Mbps ceiling slows drives
 USB-A only on the computer side
 UGREEN USB 3.0 Switch Selector, 4 Ports, One-Button
 Spec-wise this sits between the previous two: 5 Gbps class, four ports, a button on the box and two USB 3.0 cables. Next to the USB 2.0 version the difference is the link speed and the cable type, not the button or the port count, and that is the whole reason to spend a little more.
 It suits a desk where the box can live within reach, such as a shelf under a monitor riser. If the box ends up behind a computer, the controller-equipped listings are easier to live with, since you press the button daily.
 Think of it as the budget answer for a gaming desktop plus a work laptop, where a mouse, keyboard and a portable hard drive need to follow whichever machine is active. Question to ask before buying: where will the box sit? If the answer is behind the computer, price in the annoyance of reaching back there each time.
 Pros 
 5 Gbps class for drives and webcams
 Straightforward layout
 USB 3.0 cables included
 Cons

 UGREEN 2-in 7-Out USB 3.0 Switch (4 USB-A + 3 USB-C)
 Seven downstream ports is the standout. Four are USB-A and three are USB-C, so a keyboard, mouse, headset dongle, drive and a phone cable all have a place. The title also lists a USB-C male adapter and a power adapter, which matters because a supplied power adapter takes pressure off the computer’s port.
 It is the pick for a crowded dock-style desk. For a lean setup with only a keyboard and mouse it is far more hardware than necessary.
 A fitting scenario is a streaming or editing desk with a keyboard, mouse, audio interface dongle, card reader and a phone cable that all have to follow one of two computers. Question to ask before buying: how many of the seven ports will you really fill? If the answer is three or fewer, a 4-port box is cheaper and tidier.

 The layout mirrors the USB 3.0 7-out model, with four USB-A and three USB-C ports, but the title quotes 10 Gbps and USB 3.2 and says it works with A or C computers. Both the Type C converter adapter and the power adapter are named. That makes this the near-twin of the previous listing, and the speed is what you pay extra for.
 Whether the A-type ports also run at 10 Gbps is a listing question, since the title only says 10 Gbps for the switcher overall.
 Picture a desk where a fast external SSD, a mouse, a keyboard and a USB-C hub all move between a laptop and a desktop. The 10 Gbps class keeps the drive from being the bottleneck on that link. Question to ask before buying: does your fastest drive actually exceed 5 Gbps? If not, the cheaper 7-out model gives the same port layout.

 The remote is the distinguishing feature here. Title wording points to four shared ports, two USB-C data cables and an input that accepts A or C computers. Speed is not stated, so do not assume USB 3.0 or better without checking the listing.
 A remote helps when the box hides under a desk or behind a monitor arm, which is common on ergonomic setups where the surface is cleared. Whether it is wired or wireless is the other thing to confirm.
 A natural fit is a standing-desk setup where the box is clipped under the surface and a remote sits on top. Webcam and microphone are named in the title, so video calls are an intended use. Question to ask before buying: what speed does the listing state for the ports? The title leaves that open, and a drive needs the answer.

 The smallest in the group: two shared ports and two USB 3.0 cables. It handles a keyboard and a mouse, or a printer and a scanner, and not much else. The wording “printer splitter” in the title is loose; this is a switch, not a splitter, so only one computer reaches the printer at a time.
 If you already know you will add a webcam later, the 4-port versions leave room to grow without a second purchase.
 A typical home is one wireless-dongle keyboard and mouse pair that has to follow a work laptop and a desktop, nothing more. Two ports covers it and costs less than the four-port boxes. Question to ask before buying: will a webcam, headset or drive join the desk in the next year? If yes, a four-port model avoids replacing this one.

 An unusual combination: four USB devices plus a built-in gigabit LAN adapter, with two USB cables and a controller. The idea is that a single wired network connection follows the keyboard and mouse from one computer to the other. That helps a laptop without an Ethernet jack, or a desk with one wall jack.
 Network and USB devices share the same upstream link, so a big drive copy and a large download compete. Driver support for the adapter on each operating system is a listing question.
 Consider a small apartment desk with one wall jack and two computers, where a wired connection beats weak Wi-Fi for video calls. One cable from the wall goes into the switch and the active computer gets it automatically. Question to ask before buying: do both of your operating systems have a driver for the network chip, or will it install itself?

 An all-USB-C laptop pair is the target buyer. An older desktop with USB-A only would need an adapter that is not mentioned in the title.
 The matching scenario is two USB-C laptops, one personal and one from an employer, sharing a keyboard, mouse and portable SSD at a single workstation. The C-to-C cables mean nothing extra to buy.  The title advertises file sync and cross-screen drag, which implies a data link between the two computers rather than only a shared peripheral switch. Four USB 3.2 Gen 2 ports and a controller are listed. Treat the sync feature as something to verify: the title does not say whether it needs software, which operating systems it supports or how fast it runs.
 Anyone who simply wants a keyboard and mouse switch can ignore the extra and take a cheaper model.
 It could appeal to someone who moves screenshots, documents and project files between a laptop and a desktop all day and would like to skip cloud uploads. Question to ask before buying: does the feature rely on an app, and does it support both of your operating systems? Without those answers, treat the listing as a fast 4-port switch that may also move files.

 How to choose
 Match the link speed to what you plug in
 Keyboards, mice and printers are fine on USB 2.0. Webcams are usually fine on a 5 Gbps link. Storage is where the ceiling shows up. The table below shows rough ceilings; real transfers are lower, and the figures are general standards knowledge, hedged accordingly.
 Link class Nominal rate Rough theoretical ceiling Fits 
 USB 2.0 480 Mbps Roughly 60 MB/s Input devices, printers, scanners 
 USB 3.0 / 3.2 Gen 1 5 Gbps Roughly 500 MB/s Webcams, SATA SSDs, hard drives 
 USB 3.2 Gen 2 10 Gbps Roughly 1 GB/s Fast NVMe enclosures 
 Count ports and cable ends before checkout
 Draw your desk on paper: two computers on one side, devices on the other. Each computer needs a cable that fits one of its ports, and each device needs a spot on the switch. USB-C and USB-A ports are not interchangeable without an adapter, which is why the cable bundle in each title counts as much as the port count.
 Controller, remote or button
 You will press it dozens of times a week, so reach matters. A button on the box suits a shelf. A controller or remote suits a desk with the box tucked away. Ergonomically, one clear press beats twisting to find a button behind a monitor.
 Power and heat
 Bus-powered switches draw from the active computer. Models that list a power adapter supply their own. If you plan on charging a phone or running a bus-powered drive, look for an adapter in the title or a drive with its own supply.

On the data side, 4.6 Gbps sits close to the usable ceiling of a 5 Gbps link, so the 10 Gbps class gives breathing room if the drive and the webcam run together.

 Two more worth stating plainly. Do not treat near-duplicate listings as different products: the USB 2.0 and USB 3.0 one-button boxes share a layout, and the link speed is what differs. And do not count a sync feature as essential unless you have a reason to move files directly between computers.
 Verdict by use case
 For a typical shared desk, the 4-port USB 3.0 switch with a controller balances cost and flexibility. For printers and input devices only, the USB 2.0 box is plenty. For two USB-C laptops, the USBC 10 Gbps switch with C-to-C cables skips adapters. For a busy accessory desk, the two 7-out models bring their own power. The file-sync and Ethernet versions are specialists; choose them only if their extra feature solves a problem you actually have.

 Frequently asked questions
 Do I need a powered USB switch?
 It depends on what hangs off the downstream ports. A keyboard and mouse draw very little, so a bus-powered switch is usually fine. Add a bus-powered portable drive, a webcam and a phone that charges over USB, and the combined draw can pass what one upstream port supplies. Models whose titles list a power adapter remove that worry. If a drive keeps disconnecting, check power before blaming the cable.
 Will a USB 3.0 switch slow down my external SSD?
 It can cap it. A 5 Gbps link tops out near 500 MB/s in theory, and real transfers land lower, so a fast NVMe enclosure can be held back. Every device also shares the active computer’s upstream link, so a webcam running during a copy takes a slice. If drive speed matters, pick a 10 Gbps listing or plug the drive straight into the computer.
 Can one switch share a monitor as well?
 No. These are USB switches, so they move USB devices only. Video has to be switched separately, either by a KVM, a monitor with multiple inputs and a built-in USB hub, or by pressing the input button on the display. Many people pair a USB switch with a monitor’s input button and just press both when changing computers, which takes a second or two.
 Is it safe to press the button while a drive is copying?
 Avoid it. Switching disconnects the drive from one computer and presents it to the other, which interrupts any transfer in progress and can leave the file system in a bad state. Finish the copy, eject the drive in the operating system, then switch. Keyboards, mice and webcams are far less sensitive and reconnect within a moment or two, so those can follow the button freely.
 Does a USB switch work between a USB-C laptop and a USB-A desktop?
 Only when the listing includes the right inputs. Several titles here bundle two cables of different types or add a USB-C male adapter, so one computer can use USB-C while the other uses USB-A. Count the cable ends in the box against your two computers before ordering, and confirm that your laptop port carries data and is not a charge-only connector.
 Do keyboard shortcuts or hotkeys work for switching?
 The titles describe a button, controller or remote, not a keyboard hotkey. If hotkey switching matters to you, treat it as unconfirmed and check the listing, because USB switches and KVM switches differ on this point.

 Its compact body is easy to place near a shared printer, scanner, or audio interface. It also works with a USB hub, but the switch is bus powered, so a powered hub is the safer route when several attached devices need meaningful current.

 An optional Micro-USB input can supplement power for attached devices. As with the IOGEAR, that input supports the USB peripherals; it does not provide USB-C Power Delivery to a laptop or carry a display signal.
 Choose it when one host has only USB-C data ports and you want the correct cable included. Skip it if both computers already have USB-A and the limited remaining Amazon stock makes another four-port model easier to replace later.
 Who Should Buy What
 Before choosing a keyboard to share, check its actual connection mode. Our mechanical keyboards for developers guide distinguishes USB-data models from charging-only wireless keyboards and links each manufacturer’s configuration software. A USB-C socket alone does not establish compatibility with a USB switch.
 For four shared USB 3.0 devices: choose the IOGEAR GUS432 .
 For basic keyboards, mice, and printers: the UGREEN 30767 keeps four ports without paying for bandwidth those devices will not use.
 For one device or a powered hub: choose the well-documented Plugable USB3-SWITCH2 .
 For a USB-C host computer: the Monoprice 38298 includes a USB-C host cable, but it still does not carry video or charging.
 For shared monitors as well as peripherals: use a full HDMI KVM switch . For two USB-C laptops, check our USB-C KVM display, charging and software comparison first: a peripheral switch does not add video, and a dual-output MST model does not give a Mac two independent external desktops.
 Good cable routing matters more once two host cables and several peripherals meet at one box. Our desk cable-management guide covers trays, sleeves, and under-desk mounting options.
 FAQ
 Is a USB switch the same as a KVM switch?
 No. A USB switch moves USB peripherals between computers but normally has no video path. A KVM switch handles keyboard, video, and mouse together so the computers can also share a monitor.
 Can two computers use the shared USB devices at the same time?
 No. One host controls the switch at a time. Pressing the button disconnects the peripheral set from one computer and presents it to the other.
 Can I connect a USB hub to a one-port switch?
 Yes, when the switch and hub are compatible. Use a powered hub for several devices or higher power loads, and remember that every connected device shares the switch’s bandwidth and host connection.
 Will a USB switch carry video from a USB-C dock?
 Usually not. USB-C docks often depend on DisplayPort Alt Mode and Power Delivery, which ordinary USB-A data switches do not pass. Use a purpose-built USB-C KVM or Thunderbolt setup when the dock carries monitors and charging.
 Is it safe to switch an external drive between computers?
 Only after the operating system has finished writing and the drive has been safely ejected or unmounted. Switching while storage is active is equivalent to unplugging it and can corrupt files or the file system.
 Bottom Line
 The IOGEAR GUS432 is the strongest general USB switch for a two-computer desk because it combines four USB 3.0 ports with a wired selector. Choose a one-port Plugable or Sabrent when the job is smaller, and move to a true KVM when the monitor must switch too.

 Buying Guide
 Decide whether you need USB switching or a full KVM
 USB switching and video switching are separate functions. You use a USB selector to move peripherals such as keyboards, mice, scanners, and webcams between computers. It does not normally move a monitor image, so a desk that needs one display for two laptops requires a KVM or a separate plan for display inputs.
 Buy for the actual handoff you repeat. If you only move a keyboard and mouse, a compact two-port box is easier to understand. If you regularly move four or more peripherals, the UGREEN 4-port switch gives a more flexible starting layout.
 Count ports and connector types honestly
 USB-A and USB-C accessories need different physical ports. A modern desk can mix both, so a switch with the right connector types may save adapters and strain on cables. Do not choose based only on the number printed on the box if the ports do not match the devices you own.
 Leave a port free when the desk changes often. A four-port model is often enough for keyboard, mouse, webcam, and one rotating device. The seven-port option only makes sense when you can name the devices it will support and understand their power and bandwidth needs.
 Keep demanding hardware on a separate path
 External drives, audio interfaces, and capture hardware can have stricter requirements than a keyboard or mouse. A simple USB sharing switch may work for them, but test the exact device rather than making it part of a critical workflow on assumption.
 Powered docks are built for a different desk problem. If each laptop needs charging, display output, Ethernet, and peripheral expansion, look at our Thunderbolt dock guide first. A USB switch can still sit beside that dock for one intentional handoff of shared peripherals. Our USB-C cable guide can help when a data cable is the weak link.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can a USB switch share one keyboard and mouse between two laptops?
 Yes, sharing a keyboard and mouse is the core job of these products. The devices stay connected to the switch, while the selected host changes. The setup is useful when you move between two laptops but want one familiar input set.
 The change is not necessarily instant inside every application, so save work before swapping an active peripheral in a time-sensitive task. Keep the switch where you can reach it without moving both laptops.
 Will a USB sharing switch switch my monitor too?
 Usually no. USB peripheral switching does not imply HDMI, DisplayPort, or USB-C video switching. A monitor needs its own input selection or a KVM that explicitly includes video support.
 For a single-screen desk, decide whether you need a USB switch plus manual monitor input selection, or one KVM with video support. The answer depends on whether frequent monitor switching is part of your daily routine.
 Can I connect external drives to a USB switch?
 Possibly, but use care. Storage devices can need more power and stable bandwidth than a keyboard or mouse, and disconnecting during a transfer can corrupt work. Check the switch documentation and test any important drive before relying on it.
 For backup or editing storage, a direct connection or a properly powered dock is often safer. A sharing switch is most predictable when it moves low-risk desk accessories.
 Bottom Line
 The UGREEN 4-port switch is the flexible pick for a mixed USB-C and USB-A desk. Choose the 7-port USB switch when several accessories must move together, or the BENFEI 4-port switch for a conventional USB-A setup. In every case, treat the switch as a peripheral handoff and plan display, charging, and high-power devices separately.

 What Owners Should Expect From Each One
 These notes come straight from the makers’ manuals and product pages, so they describe documented behavior at the desk.
 AV Access iDock C20
 Switching takes two to three seconds, AV Access says, and the front button is the only built-in control. A wired remote exists but costs extra. If the picture flickers on a Windows laptop with Intel integrated graphics, the maker’s fix is to hold both monitors at 1080p60. On a Mac, plan on one extended display and a mirrored second one.
 Cable Matters 201085
 Expect the monitors to blink on every switch. With no EDID emulation, Cable Matters warns that displays may disconnect or rearrange afterward, so windows can land on the wrong screen. The RF remote is handy if the box sits behind a monitor. Support is a year of warranty plus lifetime tech support.
 IOGEAR GCS1602CC
 The charging rule trips people up. Only port 1 passes up to 100W, and the charger is yours; port 2 gives 5V 3A at most. Label the cables so the laptop that needs the power always goes in port 1. The 12V adapter comes in the box.
 StarTech SV211HDUC
 Simplicity is the pitch. There’s one button, no hotkey and no on-screen menu, and the box runs off the host laptop. StarTech includes two 1 m USB-C cables but not the HDMI cable, so budget for one.
 Real-World Performance
 Every USB KVM switch here makes the same trade: one set of peripherals and one or two monitors, shared by two laptops. What changes is how much else the box does while it’s there.
 Who Charges What
 Charging splits the field. The iDock C20 delivers up to 60W to each laptop at once. The IOGEAR GCS1602CC delivers up to 100W on port 1 only. The Cable Matters and StarTech boxes don’t pass power, so each laptop stays on its own charger. If both laptops are thin-and-light machines that live on USB-C power, that settles the shortlist before anything else does.
 USB C KVM Switch Dual Monitor: What Works
 Two monitors over one USB-C cable is the part that trips people up. On Windows and Linux, the Cable Matters and the AV Access box both split a single USB-C connection into two displays using DisplayPort MST, so the laptop’s port has to support DisplayPort Alt Mode and MST. On a Mac, both makers say one display extends and the second mirrors. If you need two extended screens on a Mac, a USB-C KVM like these won’t do it. Our KVM switch for dual monitors page covers the wider options.
 Mac and Windows on the Same Box
 Each input is just a USB-C host, so a Mac and a Windows laptop can share the C20 or the Cable Matters box. Expect the Mac side to follow the mirror rule above. IOGEAR lists MacBooks on macOS 10.12 or newer, and StarTech lists macOS and iPadOS. Check your own Mac’s display limit too, because the lower of the two limits is the one you get.
 Thunderbolt KVM Switch: What the Makers Say
 A Thunderbolt KVM switch is a different class of device, and none of these four is one. Cable Matters calls its switch compatible with Thunderbolt 3, 4 and 5 laptops as long as the video leaves over DisplayPort Alt Mode. IOGEAR names Thunderbolt 3 and 4 hosts. StarTech says Thunderbolt 3 only, and the AV Access page makes no Thunderbolt statement. So a Thunderbolt laptop works as a plain USB-C host here, and the USB ports top out at 5Gbps.
 Can You Plug a KVM Switch Into a Docking Station?
 The iDock C20 is the dock, which removes the question. If you already own a Thunderbolt 4 or 5 dock, the wiring matters: a non-Thunderbolt KVM switch like these can’t sit between a computer and that dock. Our Best KVM Switch (2026) shows the wiring that works instead, and the Thunderbolt 4 vs USB-C docks guide explains which port your laptop actually has.

 FAQ
 What is a USB KVM switch?
 A USB KVM switch shares one keyboard, one mouse and, in the KVM versions, one or two monitors between computers. A plain USB switch only moves the peripherals, so you’d still change the monitor input by hand.
 Do I need a USB-C KVM for a laptop with only USB-C ports?
 Yes, or a dock that does the same job. The laptop has to send video out of the USB-C port, which means DisplayPort Alt Mode, USB4 or Thunderbolt. If your laptop also has HDMI, the general KVM roundup’s HDMI picks may be cheaper.
 Can a KVM switch charge my laptop?
 Two of these can. The AV Access iDock C20 supplies up to 60W to each laptop, and the IOGEAR GCS1602CC supplies up to 100W on port 1 with your own charger. The Cable Matters and StarTech boxes don’t pass power.
 Can I run two monitors from one USB-C port?
 On Windows and Linux, yes, with DisplayPort MST over a port that supports DisplayPort Alt Mode. The Cable Matters 201085 and the AV Access iDock C20 do it. On a Mac, both makers say the second monitor mirrors the first.

 The makers list it, with conditions. Cable Matters says Thunderbolt 3, 4 and 5 laptops work if video leaves over DisplayPort Alt Mode, IOGEAR names Thunderbolt 3 and 4, and StarTech names Thunderbolt 3 only.
 Is a KVM switch a security risk?
 These are consumer switches, and nothing in the manuals sells them as security devices. If you need hard isolation between networks, you want a certified secure KVM, which is a different product.

 Switching Direction and Capacity

Users with newer laptops or fast storage should prioritize USB 3.2 and USB-C compatibility.
 If three or four computers need access to the same devices, select a multi-host model with clear status indicators. For a printer or scanner shared between two systems, a bidirectional switch may be simpler than a larger hub. Finally, verify that the selected model matches your intended ports and remember that sharing USB peripherals alone will not switch your display signal.

 Choose a USB switch when you need to move USB peripherals—such as a keyboard, mouse, printer, scanner, webcam, or audio interface—between computers without moving cables. A USB-only switch changes the computer that owns those devices; it does not switch your monitor’s video signal. If video must change at the same time, use a video KVM or a monitor with a built-in KVM feature. Before buying, count the computers and peripherals, match USB generations and connector types, check auxiliary-power requirements, and verify any dock’s exact compatibility.
 Start by deciding whether you need USB sharing or video switching 
 The word “switch” is used for several different products. A USB sharing switch sits between your computers and USB peripherals. Pressing its button (or using its remote control, where provided) disconnects the peripherals from one host and connects them to another. The monitor remains connected to whichever computer or video switch is already driving it.

 Count hosts and peripherals before comparing models 
 Count the computers (host ports)
 Most small switches are designed for two computers, but the number of host connections is a model specification, not an industry standard. “Two-port” can describe two host connections, two device connections, or the manufacturer’s naming convention, so read the connection diagram and manual.
 List every computer that must share the devices. A desktop and a work laptop are two hosts even if only one is used at a time. If you later add a third computer, a two-host switch will not become a three-host switch through a cable or hub.
 Count every downstream USB device

 USB-C, docks and video features require a separate compatibility check

 When a dock may work

 When a dock is outside the switch’s scope

 Read the dock maker’s compatibility list and the switch manual together. A USB-C receptacle on both products is not evidence that charging, display output or Thunderbolt will pass through.  Common buying mistakes to avoid 
 Buying a USB switch for a video problem: USB data switching and monitor-signal switching are separate functions.

The best USB switch is the one that moves a keyboard, a mouse, and a headset between two computers in a single press without any of that, and most of the ones that do it well cost less than a game.
 This guide is built around what goes wrong with cheap switches , because that is where the money is saved or wasted.  ⚡ Key Takeaways
 A USB switch moves your keyboard, mouse, and headset between computers with one button. It does not move the monitor; that job belongs to a KVM.
 USB 2.0 is enough for input devices. Buy USB 3.0 the moment a webcam, capture card, mic interface, or external drive joins the shared set.
 Most cheap-switch failures are power failures. A switch with a dedicated power input fixes dropouts that a longer cable never will.
 Every switch of this type disconnects devices for a moment on the swap. Plan for it, and keep the game PC’s dongles plugged in directly.

 Table of Contents
 What a USB Switch Fixes and What It Does Not
 A USB switch is a box with one button. Your keyboard, mouse, headset, and whatever else you plug into it connect to one computer at a time , and the button decides which. That is the whole product, and it solves a specific problem: a gaming PC and a work laptop on the same desk, and no desire to own two of everything or to swap cables by hand every evening.
 What it does not do is move your monitor . When you press the button, the screen keeps showing whichever computer it was already showing. If you have two monitors, or one monitor with two inputs and a quick input button, that is fine and the switch is all you need. If you want the display to follow the keyboard automatically, you are shopping for a KVM instead, and our best KVM switch guide covers the ones that handle high refresh rates without choking them.
 Switch vs KVM vs Hub
 The three get confused constantly, so here is the split. A hub turns one port into several on one computer. A USB switch points a set of devices at one of two or more computers. A KVM does that and switches the video too. The prices climb in that order, and so does the number of things that can go wrong, which is why a USB switch is often the smarter buy for a desk where the monitor problem is already solved.
 If your monitor already has two inputs, you are one cheap box away from a two-computer desk.
 A hub and a switch also stack well. Plug a hub into one of the switch’s device ports and a whole cluster of low-power gadgets moves together. Our USB-C hub guide is the place to start if the laptop side of your desk is short on ports in the first place.
 Best USB Switch Picks for Two-PC Desks

Two host ports, four USB 3.0 device ports, one button , and an LED that tells you which computer currently owns the keyboard. Both host cables come in the box, so it works the moment you unpack it.
 The two details that separate it from the bargain-bin clones are the USB 3.0 ports and the USB-C power input . The first means a webcam, a capture card, or an external SSD runs at full speed on whichever computer has it. The second means a power-hungry device such as an RGB keyboard or a bus-powered drive gets its own supply instead of browning out and vanishing every few minutes, which is the most common complaint about switches at half this price.
 The power port is the feature you do not think you need until your keyboard starts disappearing.
 The limits are the ones every two-host switch shares. Devices disconnect for a moment during the swap, a third computer needs a different product, and the included cables are on the short side for a laptop parked at the far end of a wide desk. None of those are reasons to pick something else. For a PC and a laptop with a shared keyboard, mouse, and headset, this is the answer.
 UGREEN USB 2.0 Switch: Input Devices for Less
 The UGREEN USB 2.0 Switch 2-in-4-out is the same idea with USB 2.0 ports and a lower price, and it is the right buy more often than the spec sheet suggests. A keyboard, a mouse, a wired headset, and a controller receiver together use a tiny fraction of USB 2.0’s bandwidth . If those are the only things you share, USB 3.0 buys you nothing.
 It has the same one-button layout and LED, a micro-USB port for optional power, and a review pool larger than most gaming peripherals. It is the version to buy for a desk where the second computer is a work laptop that only ever needs the keyboard and mouse.
 The catch is permanent. The moment you add a webcam, a capture card, a mic interface, or an external drive to the shared set, USB 2.0 becomes the bottleneck and you are buying the USB 3.0 model anyway. Be honest about what the desk will look like in a year before you save the difference.
 StarTech 4×4 USB 3.0 Switch: When Two Hosts Is Not Enough
 The StarTech 4×4 USB 3.0 Sharing Switch is the pick for a desk that has outgrown two computers: a gaming PC, a work laptop, a capture or streaming machine, and one more. Four hosts, four USB 3.0 device ports , and a wired remote selector so the box itself can disappear behind the desk while the button sits by the keyboard. It works with Windows, macOS, and Linux without drivers.
 It is built the way network hardware is built, with a metal chassis, over-current protection on the ports, and hot-plug support, and it is priced the same way. That is the honest tradeoff. For a two-computer desk it is several times the money for capacity you will never use, which is why it is third here and not first.
 If four hosts is real for you, the alternatives are thin. The TRENDnet TK-U404 covers the same four-by-four layout for less with a smaller review pool, and the Tripp Lite 4-Port USB 3.0 Switch shares only a single device across four computers, which suits a printer more than a gaming desk.
 One more shape exists that none of the picks cover: two computers sharing a single device. The Tripp Lite 2-Port USB 3.0 Switch does exactly that for a printer, a scanner, or an external drive that both machines need and nothing else. For a gaming desk it is the wrong tool, because a keyboard and a mouse alone already need two ports, but it is the right one for a shared drive next to a desk that has its input devices sorted.
 The USB 3.0 Catch
 Every switch listing leads with a speed, and most buyers pick the faster one on instinct. The instinct is only half right. What matters is not the number on the box but which of your devices will ever notice it.
 What Input Devices Actually Use
 A keyboard reports a handful of bytes per keypress. A gaming mouse at its highest polling rate is still a trickle next to USB 2.0’s ceiling. A wired headset streams a modest audio feed in each direction. Put all three behind a USB 2.0 switch and none of them slows down, drops polling, or adds latency you can feel. This is why the cheaper pick exists and why it is not a compromise for the job it is sold for.
 Where USB 3.0 Earns Its Price
 Cameras, capture cards, mic interfaces, and storage are different. A 1080p webcam or a capture card pushes a video stream that USB 2.0 can only carry compressed or at a lower frame rate. A bus-powered SSD behind a USB 2.0 switch transfers at a fraction of its rated speed. USB-IF’s own USB 3.2 overview lays out the 5, 10, and 20Gbps tiers; a 5Gbps switch is the floor for any of those devices, and it is what both USB 3.0 picks here run.
 Buy USB 3.0 for the camera and the drive. The keyboard will never know the difference.
 If you want to go past 5Gbps, the UGREEN 2-in-7-out USB 3.2 Switch runs seven device ports at 10Gbps and adds USB-C on both the host and device sides. It costs more than twice the USB 3.0 pick, and it only pays off if you are moving large files across the switch regularly. For a keyboard, mouse, headset, and webcam, it is speed you paid for and never see.
 Where Cheap Switches Fail
 The one-star reviews on USB switches repeat four stories. All four are avoidable, and knowing them before you buy is worth more than any spec.
 The Dropout Problem Is a Power Problem
 The most common failure is a device that randomly disconnects: the keyboard goes dead for a second, the mouse cursor freezes, a drive unmounts mid-copy. It reads like a bad switch. It is almost always power . The switch draws from the host computer’s port, and four devices plus an RGB keyboard can pull more than that port wants to give, especially on a laptop.
 The fix is the dedicated power input , which is why both UGREEN picks have one and why it is the first thing to use if anything flickers. A phone charger into that port ends the problem on most desks. Switches without a power input, which includes many of the cheapest listings, have no fix at all.
 The Swap Delay and Dongles
 Every switch of this type physically disconnects the devices from one host and connects them to the other, and the new host has to recognize them again. That takes a moment, and on the first swap after a boot it can take longer. It is normal. What is not normal is doing it during a match, so treat the button as something you press between sessions, not between rounds .
 Wireless dongles deserve their own rule. A mouse or headset receiver behind a switch re-pairs on every swap, which can add a beat of lag or a burst of static, and a few receivers refuse to wake at all until unplugged. If a wireless device belongs to the gaming PC alone, plug its receiver straight into that PC and leave the switch for the shared gear.
 Keyboards That Vanish at Boot
 Some motherboards do not initialize a switched keyboard early enough to get into the BIOS, and a few sleep-and-wake cycles can leave the switch pointed at a computer that is off. Neither is a defect in the switch. Keep a spare wired keyboard in a drawer for the rare BIOS visit, and press the button once after waking a machine that has been asleep for a while. If the desk rearranges often, a switch with a remote selector, like the StarTech, is easier to live with than one whose button ends up behind a monitor.
 Three Switches Side by Side
 The decision in one place: how many machines, how many devices, and whether you need the speed.

 UGREEN USB 3.0 Switch 2-in-4-out 2 4 USB 3.0, 5Gbps USB-C, optional A PC and a laptop sharing input devices plus a webcam or drive

 If you are stuck between the two UGREENs, list what will be plugged into the shared ports a year from now. A camera or a drive on that list means USB 3.0. Nothing but input devices means the cheaper one, with no regret.
 Setting Up a Switch Without Surprises
 A USB switch takes five minutes to install and a few small decisions to install well. Get these right the first time and you will not think about the box again.
 Put the switch where the button is reachable without looking, ideally just past the keyboard on the side the laptop lives. Measure the host cable runs before you buy longer ones; the included cables reach a tower under the desk and a laptop beside the monitor, and not much further. Use a port on the back of the PC rather than a front-panel one, which is often shared with other headers and drops power under load. And plug the power input in from the start rather than waiting for a dropout to prompt it.
 Check the laptop side before you order. All three picks use USB-A host cables, and a thin laptop with only USB-C ports needs a small USB-C to USB-A adapter or a hub on that end. It is a five-dollar problem, but it is the one that leaves the switch sitting in its box on the first evening. The switch itself does not care which side is the laptop; either host port works for either machine.
 Shared gear goes through the switch. Gaming-only gear plugs straight into the gaming PC.
 Decide which devices are truly shared. The keyboard, mouse, and a wired headset usually are. A wireless mouse receiver, a controller dongle, and a USB DAC that only the gaming PC uses should bypass the switch entirely, both to avoid the re-pair on every swap and to keep the game PC’s audio chain stable.
 If your desk is short on cable room for all of that, our desk accessories guide covers the cable management that keeps a two-computer setup tidy, and the L-shaped desk guide is where to look if two machines simply do not fit on one straight run. For anyone building the whole desk from nothing, the beginner gaming setup guide shows where a switch fits in the order of purchases.
 Finally, the monitor. If it has two inputs, connect one to each computer and learn the input button on the monitor’s menu. That single habit, plus the switch, turns a PC and a laptop into a desk that feels like one machine, at a fraction of the cost of a KVM that can keep up with a high-refresh panel. StarTech’s own explainer on what a KVM switch is is the place to go when the monitor button stops being enough.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 The questions that come up most when adding a second computer to a gaming desk.
 What is the difference between a USB switch and a KVM switch?
 A USB switch moves your keyboard, mouse, and other USB devices between computers with one button. A KVM does the same and also switches the monitor. If your monitor has two inputs and its own input button, a USB switch does the job for a fraction of the cost. If you want the screen to follow the keyboard automatically, you need a KVM.
 Do I need a USB 3.0 switch for a keyboard and mouse?
 No. Keyboards, mice, controllers, and wired headsets use a tiny fraction of USB 2.0 bandwidth, so a USB 2.0 switch handles them without any added latency. USB 3.0 matters when you share a webcam, a capture card, a mic interface, or an external drive, all of which are throttled behind USB 2.0 ports.
 Why does my keyboard disconnect when using a USB switch?
 Usually power, not the switch. Four devices drawing from one host port can exceed what that port supplies, especially on a laptop. Plug a charger into the switch’s power input, use a rear port on the PC rather than a front-panel one, and keep power-hungry gear like RGB keyboards on the powered switch rather than an unpowered clone.
 Does a USB switch add input lag for gaming?
 Not in normal use. The switch passes signals straight through, and a keyboard or mouse behind it polls at its full rate. The only delay is during the swap itself, when devices disconnect from one computer and reconnect to the other, which is why you press the button between sessions rather than mid-match.
 Should I put a wireless mouse dongle through a USB switch?
 Only if both computers need that mouse. A receiver behind a switch re-pairs on every swap, which can add a moment of lag or a burst of static, and some receivers need to be unplugged to wake. If the wireless mouse belongs to the gaming PC alone, plug its dongle straight into the PC and share the wired gear through the switch.

 Key Buying Factors for USB Switch Boxes for Windows 
 Port Count and Connector Type 
 Choose enough downstream ports for every device you want to share, including accessories you may add later. USB-A remains common for keyboards, mice, printers, and scanners, while USB-C ports are useful for newer laptops and peripherals. Check whether the listed USB-C ports are for data, host connections, or power before ordering.
 Speed and Device Compatibility 
 USB 2.0 is generally adequate for input devices and many printers. Choose USB 3.0 or USB 3.2 for external SSDs, card readers, webcams, and other bandwidth-sensitive equipment. Actual performance depends on the computers, cables, and connected device, so a faster switch cannot overcome slower hardware.
 Switching Method and Power 
 A front button is simple and reliable, while a wired button or IR remote can make switching easier when the box is out of reach. Bus-powered models keep installations tidy, but powered options may be preferable when several demanding devices or power-hungry accessories are connected.
 Windows Setup and Limitations 
 Most switches work as plug-and-play USB hubs, but some devices may reconnect slowly after switching. If you need to share displays, audio, or USB peripherals together, select a true KVM switch rather than a USB-only selector.
